claim: UPF1 is an RNA helicase that is required for nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD) in eukaryotes.
source: UPF1 is an RNA helicase that is required for nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD) in eukaryotes, and the predominant view is that UPF1 mainly operates on the 3'UTRs of mRNAs that are directed for NMD in the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field, supported by citations throughout the manuscript and presented as background knowledge.

claim: The predominant view is that UPF1 mainly operates on the 3'UTRs of mRNAs that are directed for NMD in the cytoplasm.
source: UPF1 is an RNA helicase that is required for nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD) in eukaryotes, and the predominant view is that UPF1 mainly operates on the 3'UTRs of mRNAs that are directed for NMD in the cytoplasm.
evidence: This represents the prevailing scientific view in the field, as indicated by the phrase 'predominant view'.

claim: UPF1 constantly moves between the nucleus and cytoplasm by a mechanism that requires its RNA helicase activity.
source: Here we offer evidence, obtained from Drosophila, that UPF1 constantly moves between the nucleus and cytoplasm by a mechanism that requires its RNA helicase activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from FLIP and FRAP experiments, and LMB treatment experiments showing that the DE617AA mutant (lacking helicase activity) does not relocalize.

claim: UPF1 is associated, genome-wide, with nascent RNAs at most of the active Pol II transcription sites.
source: UPF1 is associated, genome-wide, with nascent RNAs at most of the active Pol II transcription sites and at some Pol III-transcribed genes, as demonstrated microscopically on the polytene chromosomes of salivary glands and by ChIP-seq analysis in S2 cells.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data and immunofluorescence microscopy on polytene chromosomes shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: UPF1 is associated with nascent RNAs at some Pol III-transcribed genes.
source: UPF1 is associated, genome-wide, with nascent RNAs at most of the active Pol II transcription sites and at some Pol III-transcribed genes, as demonstrated microscopically on the polytene chromosomes of salivary glands and by ChIP-seq analysis in S2 cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated by ChIP-seq data showing UPF1 association with 7SK and 7SL snRNA genes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).

claim: Intron recognition seems to interfere with association and translocation of UPF1 on nascent pre-mRNAs.
source: Intron recognition seems to interfere with association and translocation of UPF1 on nascent pre-mRNAs, and cells depleted of UPF1 show defects in the release of mRNAs from transcription sites and their export from the nucleus.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data showing higher UPF1 enrichment in exons compared to introns, and by experiments showing that U1-70K depletion abolishes this bias.

claim: Cells depleted of UPF1 show defects in the release of mRNAs from transcription sites.
source: Intron recognition seems to interfere with association and translocation of UPF1 on nascent pre-mRNAs, and cells depleted of UPF1 show defects in the release of mRNAs from transcription sites and their export from the nucleus.
evidence: This is demonstrated by oligo(dT) FISH experiments showing poly(A) RNA accumulation at transcription sites in UPF1-depleted cells (Figure 6).

claim: Cells depleted of UPF1 show defects in the export of mRNAs from the nucleus.
source: Intron recognition seems to interfere with association and translocation of UPF1 on nascent pre-mRNAs, and cells depleted of UPF1 show defects in the release of mRNAs from transcription sites and their export from the nucleus.
evidence: This is demonstrated by oligo(dT) FISH showing nuclear accumulation of poly(A) RNA in UPF1-depleted cells (Figure 6A).

claim: UPF1 was first identified in a Saccharomyces cerevisiae genetic screen for mutations that enhance up-frameshift tRNA suppression.
source: UPF1 (UP-Frameshift-1) is a universally conserved eukaryotic protein that was first identified in a Saccharomyces cerevisiae genetic screen for mutations that enhance up-frameshift tRNA suppression (Culbertson et al., 1980; Leeds et al., 1992), and gained other names – including NAM7 (S. cerevisiae) and SMG2 (Caenorhabditis elegans) – from other genetic screens (Altamura et al., 1992; Hodgkin et al., 1989; Pulak and Anderson, 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the original genetic screen publications.

claim: UPF1 gained other names including NAM7 (S. cerevisiae) and SMG2 (Caenorhabditis elegans) from other genetic screens.
source: UPF1 (UP-Frameshift-1) is a universally conserved eukaryotic protein that was first identified in a Saccharomyces cerevisiae genetic screen for mutations that enhance up-frameshift tRNA suppression (Culbertson et al., 1980; Leeds et al., 1992), and gained other names – including NAM7 (S. cerevisiae) and SMG2 (Caenorhabditis elegans) – from other genetic screens (Altamura et al., 1992; Hodgkin et al., 1989; Pulak and Anderson, 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the relevant genetic screen publications.

claim: Cells that lack active UPF1 accumulate mRNAs with nonsense, frameshift or other mutant alleles that introduce a premature translation termination codon (PTC).
source: Cells that lack active UPF1 accumulate mRNAs with nonsense, frameshift or other mutant alleles that introduce a premature translation termination codon (PTC) (Leeds et al., 1991; Pulak and Anderson, 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies demonstrating this phenotype.

claim: UPF1 and related proteins are primarily required for nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD).
source: These observations are generally interpreted as evidence that UPF1 and related proteins are primarily required for nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD), a conserved eukaryotic mRNA surveillance mechanism that detects and destroys mRNAs on which translation terminates prematurely (Fatscher et al., 2015; He and Jacobson, 2015; Karousis et al., 2016; Kurosaki and Maquat, 2016).
evidence: This represents the general interpretation in the field, supported by multiple review citations.

claim: NMD is a conserved eukaryotic mRNA surveillance mechanism that detects and destroys mRNAs on which translation terminates prematurely.
source: These observations are generally interpreted as evidence that UPF1 and related proteins are primarily required for nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD), a conserved eukaryotic mRNA surveillance mechanism that detects and destroys mRNAs on which translation terminates prematurely (Fatscher et al., 2015; He and Jacobson, 2015; Karousis et al., 2016; Kurosaki and Maquat, 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by multiple review citations.

claim: NMD is mainly regarded as a quality control mechanism that prevents cells from wastefully making truncated (and potentially toxic) proteins.
source: NMD is mainly regarded as a quality control mechanism that prevents cells from wastefully making truncated (and potentially toxic) proteins and that regulates the selective expression of specific mRNA isoforms during cell homeostasis and differentiation (Goetz and Wilkinson, 2017; Lykke-Andersen and Jensen, 2015).
evidence: This represents the prevailing view in the field, supported by review citations.

claim: NMD regulates the selective expression of specific mRNA isoforms during cell homeostasis and differentiation.
source: NMD is mainly regarded as a quality control mechanism that prevents cells from wastefully making truncated (and potentially toxic) proteins and that regulates the selective expression of specific mRNA isoforms during cell homeostasis and differentiation (Goetz and Wilkinson, 2017; Lykke-Andersen and Jensen, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by review citations discussing the regulatory roles of NMD.

claim: Standard models postulate that UPF1 monitors translation termination on ribosomes by interacting with a peptide release factor (eRF1 or eRF3).
source: Standard models postulate that UPF1 monitors translation termination on ribosomes by interacting with a peptide release factor (eRF1 or eRF3).
evidence: This represents the standard model in the field, as indicated by the phrase 'standard models postulate'.

claim: Recent reports on mammalian translation systems have suggested that UPF1 does not bind to either eRF1 or eRF3, in contrast to earlier reports on other organisms.
source: However, recent reports on mammalian translation systems have suggested, in contrast to earlier reports on other organisms (Czaplinski et al., 1998; Ivanov et al., 2008; Kashima et al., 2006; Keeling et al., 2004; Singh et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2001), that UPF1 does not bind to either of these.
evidence: This is supported by citations to both recent and earlier conflicting reports.

claim: Recent reports suggested that UPF3B may contact release factors, slow the termination of translation and facilitate post-termination release of ribosomes.
source: They suggested, instead, that UPF3B may contact release factors, slow the termination of translation and facilitate post-termination release of ribosomes – and so fulfil the termination monitoring role that has been assigned to UPF1 (Neu-Yilik et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a recent study.

claim: UPF1 is an ATP-driven helicase that unwinds RNA secondary structures.
source: UPF1 is an ATP-driven helicase that unwinds RNA secondary structures and so can displace RNA-bound proteins (Bhattacharya et al., 2000; Chakrabarti et al., 2011; Czaplinski et al., 1995; Fiorini et al., 2015; Franks et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to biochemical studies.

claim: UPF1 can displace RNA-bound proteins.
source: UPF1 is an ATP-driven helicase that unwinds RNA secondary structures and so can displace RNA-bound proteins (Bhattacharya et al., 2000; Chakrabarti et al., 2011; Czaplinski et al., 1995; Fiorini et al., 2015; Franks et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to biochemical studies.

claim: UPF1 is predominantly associated with 3'UTRs of cytoplasmic mRNAs.
source: UPF1 is predominantly associated with 3'UTRs of cytoplasmic mRNAs which indicates that it might be selectively recruited to or activated on NMD targets with abnormally long 3'UTRs (Karousis et al., 2016; Kurosaki and Maquat, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies showing this association pattern.

claim: UPF1 appears to bind mRNAs fairly indiscriminately, regardless of the position of the stop codon or the PTC.
source: However, UPF1 appears to bind mRNAs fairly indiscriminately, regardless of the position of the stop codon or the PTC and whether or not the mRNA possess NMD-inducing features such as an abnormally long 3'UTR or an exon junction downstream of the stop codon (Hogg and Goff, 2010; Hurt et al., 2013; Zünd et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies showing broad UPF1 binding patterns.

claim: UPF1 helicase activity is required for NMD.
source: UPF1 helicase activity is required for NMD, but how it helps to target particular transcripts for NMD remains unclear.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: It has been questioned whether cells do possess any mechanism to discriminate between PTCs and normal stop codons.
source: In view of these and other perplexing observations, it has also been questioned whether cells do possess any such mechanism to discriminate between PTCs and normal stop codons (Brogna et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review questioning this mechanism.

claim: UPF1 is most abundant in the cytoplasm.
source: UPF1 is most abundant in the cytoplasm where its roles discussed above depend on ribosomal translation and occur on cytoplasmic mRNAs.
evidence: This is supported by cell fractionation data (Figure 1C) and immunofluorescence data (Figure 1D).

claim: A fraction of UPF1 was expected in the nucleus, as the protein traffics in and out of the nucleus in mammalian cells.
source: A fraction of UPF1 was expected in the nucleus though, as the protein traffics in and out of the nucleus in mammalian cells (Ajamian et al., 2015; Mendell et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies in mammalian cells.

claim: Some studies have concluded that within the nucleus UPF1 plays a distinct and direct role in DNA replication.
source: Some studies have concluded that within the nucleus UPF1 plays a distinct and direct role in DNA replication, which would be unrelated to gene expression (Azzalin and Lingner, 2006; Azzalin et al., 2007; Carastro et al., 2002; Chawla et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies proposing this role.

claim: The negative effects that depletion of UPF1 has on DNA replication and cell division could be an indirect consequence of NMD suppression altering the expression of genes required in such processes.
source: However, the negative effects that depletion of UPF1 has on DNA replication and cell division could be an indirect consequence of NMD suppression altering the expression of genes required in such processes (Varsally and Brogna, 2012).
evidence: This is an alternative interpretation supported by a citation.

claim: There is evidence that nuclear UPF1 might contribute directly to RNA processing, at least in specific instances.
source: Moreover, there is evidence that nuclear UPF1 might contribute directly to RNA processing, at least in specific instances, and is required for nuclear export of HIV-1 genomic RNA in HeLa cells (Ajamian et al., 2015; de Turris et al., 2011; Flury et al., 2014; Varsally and Brogna, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies showing these roles.

claim: UPF1 is required for nuclear export of HIV-1 genomic RNA in HeLa cells.
source: Moreover, there is evidence that nuclear UPF1 might contribute directly to RNA processing, at least in specific instances, and is required for nuclear export of HIV-1 genomic RNA in HeLa cells (Ajamian et al., 2015; de Turris et al., 2011; Flury et al., 2014; Varsally and Brogna, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a study in HeLa cells.

claim: CLIP data indicate direct binding of UPF1 with the abundant nuclear-localised metastasis-associated lung adenocarcinoma transcript 1 (MALAT1) in mammalian cells.
source: Additionally, CLIP data indicate direct binding of UPF1 with the abundant nuclear-localised metastasis-associated lung adenocarcinoma transcript 1 (MALAT1) in mammalian cells (Zünd et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to CLIP data.

claim: Three monoclonal anti-peptide antibodies were generated that target regions of Drosophila UPF1 outside the RNA helicase domain.
source: To explore the functions of UPF1, we generated three monoclonal anti-peptide antibodies that target regions of Drosophila UPF1 outside the RNA helicase domain: one epitope in the N-terminal flanking regions (antibody 1C13 against Pep2), and two near the C-terminus (Ab 7D17 vs. Pep11; and Ab 7B12 vs. Pep12) (see Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach taken by the authors.

claim: Each antibody detected UPF1 as a single band by western blotting of Drosophila S2 cell extracts, with minimal cross-reactivity to other proteins.
source: Following purification from hybridoma supernatants, each antibody detected UPF1 as a single band by western blotting of Drosophila S2 cell extracts, with minimal cross-reactivity to other proteins (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by western blot data shown in the figures.

claim: The antibodies detected a second, larger band of the expected molecular weight in extracts from transfected S2 cells that over-express UPF1-GFP.
source: The antibodies also detected a second, larger band of the expected molecular weight in extracts from transfected S2 cells that over-express UPF1-GFP.
evidence: This is shown in western blot data (Figure 1A).

claim: UPF1-RNAi specifically reduced the amount of UPF1 in S2 cells without affecting the levels of several other proteins tested as controls.
source: As expected, UPF1-RNAi specifically reduced the amount of UPF1 in S2 cells without affecting the levels of several other proteins we tested as controls (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by western blot data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Following cell fractionation of S2 cells, a small proportion of the UPF1 co-purified with nuclei whilst most was in the cytoplasmic fraction.
source: Following cell fractionation of S2 cells, α-tubulin and RNA Pol II were, as expected, restricted to the cytoplasmic and nuclear fractions, respectively – and a small proportion of the UPF1 co-purified with nuclei whilst most was in the cytoplasmic fraction (Figure 1C), consistent with the subcellular localisation detected by immunostaining.
evidence: This is demonstrated by cell fractionation and western blot data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: UPF1 was most abundant in the cytoplasm and perinuclear region in Drosophila salivary glands, with distinct but less intense nuclear staining.
source: UPF1 was most abundant in the cytoplasm and perinuclear region, and there was also distinct but less intense nuclear staining, mainly around the chromosomes and around the nucleolus (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: A similar subcellular distribution of UPF1 was detected with the remaining two antibodies tested in wild-type salivary glands.
source: A similar subcellular distribution of UPF1 was detected with the remaining two antibodies tested in wild-type salivary glands; and, the signal was drastically reduced in UPF1-RNAi glands, consistent with all three antibodies being specific (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The UPF1 signal was drastically reduced in UPF1-RNAi glands, consistent with all three antibodies being specific.
source: A similar subcellular distribution of UPF1 was detected with the remaining two antibodies tested in wild-type salivary glands; and, the signal was drastically reduced in UPF1-RNAi glands, consistent with all three antibodies being specific (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence data comparing wild-type and UPF1-RNAi glands.

claim: UPF1 was detected both in the cytoplasm and in the nucleus in other larval tissues, with varying immunostaining intensities.
source: UPF1 was also detected both in the cytoplasm and in the nucleus in other larval tissues, with varying immunostaining intensities.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence data in Malpighian tubules and gut (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).

claim: Perinuclear UPF1 was more apparent in salivary glands that are at a later stage of development.
source: Perinuclear UPF1 was more apparent in salivary glands that are at a later stage of development (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A); and it was also obvious in Malpighian tubules and gut, which also showed an increased intra-nuclear UPF1 signal (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence data comparing different developmental stages.

claim: In enterocytes (EC), UPF1 staining was similar between the cytoplasm and the nucleus, while the most intense UPF1 signal was perinuclear.
source: In enterocytes (EC), staining was similar between the cytoplasm and the nucleus, while the most intense UPF1 signal was perinuclear (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence data in gut tissue.

claim: UPF1 co-localised with binding of wheat germ agglutinin (WGA) in salivary glands expressing GFP-UPF1.
source: The perinuclear presence was also apparent in salivary glands expressing GFP-UPF1, where UPF1 co-localised with binding of wheat germ agglutinin (WGA) – a lectin that predominantly interacts with O-GlcNAc-modified nuclear pore proteins (Mizuguchi-Hata et al., 2013) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-localization data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: WGA is a lectin that predominantly interacts with O-GlcNAc-modified nuclear pore proteins.
source: The perinuclear presence was also apparent in salivary glands expressing GFP-UPF1, where UPF1 co-localised with binding of wheat germ agglutinin (WGA) – a lectin that predominantly interacts with O-GlcNAc-modified nuclear pore proteins (Mizuguchi-Hata et al., 2013) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: FLIP revealed that sustained photobleaching of a small area of the cytoplasm led to an initial rapid decrease in GFP-UPF1 fluorescence followed by a continued slower reduction within the continuously illuminated area.
source: FLIP revealed that sustained photobleaching of a small area of the cytoplasm led, within the continuously illuminated area, to an initial rapid decrease in GFP-UPF1fluorescence followed by a continued slower reduction.
evidence: This is demonstrated by FLIP data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Fluorescence declined steadily both elsewhere in the cytoplasm, and, more slowly, within the nucleus during FLIP experiments.
source: Fluorescence also declined steadily both elsewhere in the cytoplasm, and, more slowly, within the nucleus (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by FLIP data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Nuclear UPF1 can leave the nucleus and enter the photodepletable cytoplasmic UPF1 pool at a fairly steady rate.
source: These observations demonstrate ongoing diffusion of UPF1 throughout the cytoplasm, and that nuclear UPF1 can leave the nucleus and enter the photodepletable cytoplasmic UPF1 pool at a fairly steady rate.
evidence: This is inferred from the FLIP data showing nuclear fluorescence decline.

claim: Almost all of the UPF1 in each cell compartment was rapidly mobile, with the halftime for repopulation of each bleached area being only a few seconds.
source: Almost all of the UPF1 in each cell compartment was rapidly mobile, with the halftime for repopulation of each bleached area being only a few seconds (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by FRAP data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Nucleo-cytoplasmic shuttling has been reported in HeLa cells, with UPF1 accumulating in the nuclei following treatment with leptomycin B (LMB).
source: Nucleo-cytoplasmic shuttling has been reported in HeLa cells, with UPF1 accumulating in the nuclei following treatment with leptomycin B (LMB) (Mendell et al., 2002), a drug that selectively inhibits CRM1-mediated protein export from the nucleus in most eukaryotes (Fukuda et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies in HeLa cells.

claim: LMB is a drug that selectively inhibits CRM1-mediated protein export from the nucleus in most eukaryotes.
source: Nucleo-cytoplasmic shuttling has been reported in HeLa cells, with UPF1 accumulating in the nuclei following treatment with leptomycin B (LMB) (Mendell et al., 2002), a drug that selectively inhibits CRM1-mediated protein export from the nucleus in most eukaryotes (Fukuda et al., 1997).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: In glands treated with LMB for 60 min most of the GFP-UPF1 was observed within the nucleus, being largely excluded from the nucleolus.
source: In glands treated with LMB for 60 min most of the GFP-UPF1 was observed within the nucleus, being largely excluded from the nucleolus (Figure 2A, right panels), suggesting that UPF1 exits from the nucleus, directly or indirectly, via a CRM1-dependent mechanism.
evidence: This is demonstrated by live imaging data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: UPF1 exits from the nucleus, directly or indirectly, via a CRM1-dependent mechanism.
source: In glands treated with LMB for 60 min most of the GFP-UPF1 was observed within the nucleus, being largely excluded from the nucleolus (Figure 2A, right panels), suggesting that UPF1 exits from the nucleus, directly or indirectly, via a CRM1-dependent mechanism.
evidence: This is inferred from the LMB treatment experiment showing nuclear accumulation.

claim: UPF1 redistribution to the nucleus was rapid in living glands: UPF1 was accumulating in the nucleus by the earliest time images could be collected (within ~5–6 min from adding LMB).
source: This UPF1 redistribution was rapid in living glands: UPF1 was accumulating in the nucleus by the earliest time we could collect images (within ~5–6 min from adding LMB), and much of the cell's UPF1 localised in the nucleus within half an hour (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Much of the cell's UPF1 localised in the nucleus within half an hour of LMB treatment.
source: This UPF1 redistribution was rapid in living glands: UPF1 was accumulating in the nucleus by the earliest time we could collect images (within ~5–6 min from adding LMB), and much of the cell's UPF1 localised in the nucleus within half an hour (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by time-lapse imaging data.

claim: Both wild-type and mutant UPF1 proteins, tagged with GFP at either the N- or the C-terminal, were more abundant in the cytoplasm.
source: Both the wild type and the mutant proteins, tagged with GFP at either the N- or the C-terminal, were more abundant in the cytoplasm, as expected (Figure 2B, left panel).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data in S2 cells shown in Figure 2B.

claim: A portion of UPF1, the DA617AA mutant in particular, localised in bright fluorescent dots in the cytoplasm, possibly corresponding to P bodies.
source: A portion of UPF1, the DA617AA mutant in particular, localised in bright fluorescent dots in the cytoplasm, possibly corresponding to P bodies (Brogna et al., 2008).
evidence: This is observed in imaging data and speculated to correspond to P bodies based on a citation.

claim: Wild-type UPF1 relocalised to the nucleus following LMB treatment, resulting in more UPF1 present in the nucleus than in the cytoplasm.
source: However, whilst the wild-type UPF1 relocalised to the nucleus following the LMB treatment, resulting in more UPF1 present in the nucleus than in the cytoplasm, the distribution of the DE617AA mutants was unaffected (Figure 2B, right panel).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data comparing control and LMB-treated cells in Figure 2B.

claim: The distribution of the DE617AA mutants was unaffected by LMB treatment.
source: However, whilst the wild-type UPF1 relocalised to the nucleus following the LMB treatment, resulting in more UPF1 present in the nucleus than in the cytoplasm, the distribution of the DE617AA mutants was unaffected (Figure 2B, right panel).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data showing no change in mutant UPF1 localization after LMB treatment.

claim: Wild-type UPF1 is freely mobile within cell compartments and constantly moves in and out of the nucleus by mechanisms that involve the CRM1-dependent nuclear export pathway and requires its RNA helicase activity.
source: The data indicate that wild-type UPF1 is freely mobile within cell compartments and that it constantly moves in and out of the nucleus by mechanisms that involve the CRM1-dependent nuclear export pathway and requires its RNA helicase activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined FLIP, FRAP, and LMB treatment data with wild-type and mutant UPF1.

claim: UPF1 was present predominantly at interbands and puffs on polytene chromosomes.
source: UPF1 was present predominantly at interbands and puffs: cytologically distinct chromosome regions in which the chromatin is less condensed and that correspond to transcriptionally active sites (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence on polytene chromosomes shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Interbands and puffs are cytologically distinct chromosome regions in which the chromatin is less condensed and that correspond to transcriptionally active sites.
source: UPF1 was present predominantly at interbands and puffs: cytologically distinct chromosome regions in which the chromatin is less condensed and that correspond to transcriptionally active sites (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is established knowledge about polytene chromosome structure.

claim: UPF1-RNAi drastically depletes the endogenous UPF1 chromosomal signal.
source: The immunofluorescence signal appears to be specific, as: (a) UPF1-RNAi drastically depletes the endogenous UPF1 chromosomal signal (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B); (b) the other two UPF1 antibodies produced a similar immunostaining banding pattern (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C); and, (c) transgenically over-expressed UPF1-GFP, detected either by its fluorescence or with an anti-GFP antibody, also shows a similar banding pattern on the chromosomes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing wild-type and UPF1-RNAi chromosomes.

claim: The other two UPF1 antibodies produced a similar immunostaining banding pattern on polytene chromosomes.
source: The immunofluorescence signal appears to be specific, as: (a) UPF1-RNAi drastically depletes the endogenous UPF1 chromosomal signal (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B); (b) the other two UPF1 antibodies produced a similar immunostaining banding pattern (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C); and, (c) transgenically over-expressed UPF1-GFP, detected either by its fluorescence or with an anti-GFP antibody, also shows a similar banding pattern on the chromosomes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence with different antibodies.

claim: Transgenically over-expressed UPF1-GFP shows a similar banding pattern on the chromosomes.
source: The immunofluorescence signal appears to be specific, as: (a) UPF1-RNAi drastically depletes the endogenous UPF1 chromosomal signal (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B); (b) the other two UPF1 antibodies produced a similar immunostaining banding pattern (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C); and, (c) transgenically over-expressed UPF1-GFP, detected either by its fluorescence or with an anti-GFP antibody, also shows a similar banding pattern on the chromosomes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging of GFP-UPF1 on chromosomes.

claim: Much of the UPF1 co-localised with Ser2 Pol II on polytene chromosomes.
source: Much of the UPF1 co-localised with Ser2 Pol II, as would be expected from this type of banding pattern (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by double immunostaining shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The association of UPF1 with the chromosomes depends on transcription.
source: The association of UPF1 with the chromosomes depends on transcription. This is illustrated by the changes in UPF1 immunostaining that followed heat-shock, which induces transcription at specific cytological puffs encoding heat-shock proteins and of hsrω lncRNAs at locus 93D (Lakhotia et al., 2012).
evidence: This is demonstrated by heat-shock experiments showing UPF1 redistribution to heat-shock puffs.

claim: Heat-shock induces transcription at specific cytological puffs encoding heat-shock proteins and of hsrω lncRNAs at locus 93D.
source: The association of UPF1 with the chromosomes depends on transcription. This is illustrated by the changes in UPF1 immunostaining that followed heat-shock, which induces transcription at specific cytological puffs encoding heat-shock proteins and of hsrω lncRNAs at locus 93D (Lakhotia et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge about heat-shock response, supported by a citation.

claim: Heat-shock revealed a pattern of UPF1 association at heat shock puffs and of detachment from most other transcription sites.
source: This revealed a pattern of UPF1 association at heat shock puffs and of detachment from most other transcription sites (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence on heat-shocked chromosomes shown in Figure 3B.

claim: UPF1 was recruited to activated heat-shock genes that either contained or lacked introns.
source: UPF1 was recruited to activated heat-shock genes that either contained (33B, 63B, 64F, 67B, 70A and 93D) or lacked (87A, 87C and 95D) introns (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence showing UPF1 at various heat-shock loci.

claim: UPF1 was recruited to an ecdysone-inducible transgene (S136 at chromosomal position 63B) following transcription activation.
source: UPF1 was also recruited to other genes following transcription activation, such as to an ecdysone-inducible transgene (S136 at chromosomal position 63B), at normal temperature (Choudhury et al., 2016).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence on ecdysone-treated chromosomes shown in Figure 3C.

claim: No UPF1 was found at the S136 locus on the wild-type chromosome, but UPF1 was clearly associated with the transcription puff produced at this location following ecdysone activation of the transgene.
source: No UPF1 was found at this locus on the wild-type chromosome, but UPF1 was clearly associated with the transcription puff which was produced at this location following ecdysone activation of the transgene (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing wild-type and transgene-containing chromosomes after ecdysone treatment.

claim: UPF1 was associated with many transcriptionally active genes, most of which are Pol II transcription sites.
source: UPF1 was associated with many transcriptionally active genes, most of which are Pol II transcription sites.
evidence: This is demonstrated by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Actin5C was one of the most UPF1-enriched genes in the ChIP-seq data.
source: Actin5C provided a striking example of correspondence between the ChIP-seq and polytene immunostaining results: it was one of the most UPF1-enriched genes in the ChIP-seq data (Supplementary file 2, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B shows the UPF1 ChIP-seq profile of Actin5C) and displayed one of the brightest UPF1 chromosomal signals at the gene locus corresponding to interband 5C on the X chromosome (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ChIP-seq data in Supplementary file 2 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Actin5C displayed one of the brightest UPF1 chromosomal signals at the gene locus corresponding to interband 5C on the X chromosome.
source: Actin5C provided a striking example of correspondence between the ChIP-seq and polytene immunostaining results: it was one of the most UPF1-enriched genes in the ChIP-seq data (Supplementary file 2, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B shows the UPF1 ChIP-seq profile of Actin5C) and displayed one of the brightest UPF1 chromosomal signals at the gene locus corresponding to interband 5C on the X chromosome (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence on polytene chromosomes shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The ChIP-seq data show UPF1 association with a few Pol III genes.
source: The ChIP-seq data also show UPF1 association with a few Pol III genes (Supplementary file 2, to be discussed later).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ChIP-seq data shown in Supplementary file 2 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The enrichment profile of UPF1 at Pol II loci closely followed that of Ser2 Pol II.
source: The enrichment profile of UPF1 at Pol II loci closely followed that of Ser2 Pol II, and UPF1 enrichment being the greatest at highly expressed genes (Figure 4A; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1 show additional examples of UPF1-enriched genes).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ChIP-seq profiles shown in Figure 4A and related figures.

claim: UPF1 enrichment was greatest at highly expressed genes.
source: The enrichment profile of UPF1 at Pol II loci closely followed that of Ser2 Pol II, and UPF1 enrichment being the greatest at highly expressed genes (Figure 4A; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1 show additional examples of UPF1-enriched genes).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ChIP-seq data and metagene analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: A close correlation was observed between UPF1 and Ser2 Pol II ChIP-seq signals.
source: A close correlation was observed between UPF1 and Ser2 Pol II ChIP-seq signals, and also between UPF1-ChIP signals and mRNA levels (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by scatter plot analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: A close correlation was observed between UPF1-ChIP signals and mRNA levels.
source: A close correlation was observed between UPF1 and Ser2 Pol II ChIP-seq signals, and also between UPF1-ChIP signals and mRNA levels (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by scatter plot analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: UPF1-RNAi led to a reduction in UPF1 enrichment at transcription sites.
source: UPF1-RNAi led to a reduction in UPF1 enrichment at transcription sites, both confirming the specificity of the antibody and validating the ChIP protocol (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ChIP-qPCR data comparing control and UPF1-RNAi cells.

claim: UPF1 is associated with genes throughout their transcription units, particularly with highly expressed genes.
source: A metagene analysis of the ChIP-seq data shows that UPF1 is associated with genes, particularly with highly expressed genes (blue trace), and throughout their transcription units (Figure 4D), whereas Ser2 Pol II typically shows higher loading around transcription start sites (TSS) – corresponding to promoter-proximal Pol II pausing sites, as previously reported in Drosophila and other organisms (Adelman and Lis, 2012; Muse et al., 2007).
evidence: This is demonstrated by metagene analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Ser2 Pol II typically shows higher loading around transcription start sites (TSS) corresponding to promoter-proximal Pol II pausing sites.
source: A metagene analysis of the ChIP-seq data shows that UPF1 is associated with genes, particularly with highly expressed genes (blue trace), and throughout their transcription units (Figure 4D), whereas Ser2 Pol II typically shows higher loading around transcription start sites (TSS) – corresponding to promoter-proximal Pol II pausing sites, as previously reported in Drosophila and other organisms (Adelman and Lis, 2012; Muse et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations and demonstrated in the metagene analysis.

claim: Most gene-associated UPF1 was further downstream than the TSS-proximal Ser2 Pol II peak, especially at highly expressed genes.
source: Typically, most gene-associated UPF1 was further downstream than the TSS-proximal Ser2 Pol II peak, especially at highly expressed genes (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by metagene analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: UPF1 association depends on transcription elongation.
source: A comparison of the UPF1 loading of genes with different Ser2 Pol II loading profiles suggests that UPF1 association depends on transcription elongation: UPF1 did not associate with genes at which Ser2 Pol II was associated only with the TSS pausing site and which were not being actively transcribed (e.g. Adam TS-A, panel five in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is inferred from ChIP-seq data comparing genes with different Pol II profiles.

claim: UPF1 did not associate with genes at which Ser2 Pol II was associated only with the TSS pausing site and which were not being actively transcribed.
source: A comparison of the UPF1 loading of genes with different Ser2 Pol II loading profiles suggests that UPF1 association depends on transcription elongation: UPF1 did not associate with genes at which Ser2 Pol II was associated only with the TSS pausing site and which were not being actively transcribed (e.g. Adam TS-A, panel five in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ChIP-seq data for the Adam TS-A gene.

claim: The association of UPF1 with Pol II transcription sites is partially sensitive to RNase treatment.
source: The association of UPF1 with Pol II transcription sites is partially sensitive to RNase treatment, suggesting that UPF1 binds nascent RNA.
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNase treatment experiments on polytene chromosomes and ChIP-qPCR.

claim: UPF1 association was less sensitive to RNase treatment than that of the RNA binding protein hnRNPA1.
source: UPF1 association was, though, less sensitive to RNase treatment than that of the RNA binding protein hnRNPA1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B and C), which is almost completely detached from the chromosome following the same RNase treatment.
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing RNase sensitivity of UPF1 and hnRNPA1 on chromosomes.

claim: Some of UPF1 co-purifies with Ser2 Pol II in a standard immunoprecipitation of S2 nuclear cell extracts, the interaction being sensitive to RNase treatment.
source: Some of UPF1 co-purifies with Ser2 Pol II in a standard immunoprecipitation of S2 nuclear cell extracts, the interaction being again sensitive to RNase treatment (Figure 4—figure supplement 2E): less than that of hnRNPA1, but comparable to that of eIF4AIII, one of the exon junction complex (EJC) proteins that are loaded onto nascent RNAs (Choudhury et al., 2016).
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2E.

claim: DRB markedly reduced the amount of UPF1 associated with gene loci in salivary glands.
source: DRB treatment, as expected, left interbands and puffs cytologically unaffected, however, it markedly reduced the amount of UPF1 associated with gene loci (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D and E), providing further evidence that transcript elongation into the body of the gene is needed for this association to occur.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence on DRB-treated chromosomes.

claim: DRB reduced the association of UPF1 and Ser2 Pol II with genes in S2 cells.
source: DRB also reduced the association of UPF1 and Ser2 Pol II with genes, such as the highly expressed RpL23A, in S2 cells (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ChIP-qPCR data comparing control and DRB-treated cells.

claim: UPF1 binds at some Pol III genes including 7SK and both paralogous genes of 7SL snRNAs.
source: UPF1 was found mainly at Pol II transcription sites, most of which are protein-coding genes, however, our ChIP-seq data revealed that UPF1 also binds at some Pol III genes. The latter included 7SK and both paralogous genes of 7SL snRNAs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B) – but not, for example, the much more numerous Pol III-transcribed tRNA genes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: UPF1 does not bind to the much more numerous Pol III-transcribed tRNA genes.
source: UPF1 was found mainly at Pol II transcription sites, most of which are protein-coding genes, however, our ChIP-seq data revealed that UPF1 also binds at some Pol III genes. The latter included 7SK and both paralogous genes of 7SL snRNAs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B) – but not, for example, the much more numerous Pol III-transcribed tRNA genes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ChIP-seq data showing no UPF1 signal at tRNA genes.

claim: UPF1 was recruited both to intron-containing and intronless genes that were undergoing transcription.
source: UPF1 was recruited both to intron-containing and intronless genes that were undergoing transcription (Figure 5—figure supplement 1, and see also the earlier discussion of heat-shock gene activation), so recruitment did not depend on pre-mRNA splicing.
evidence: This is demonstrated by ChIP-seq data and heat-shock experiments.

claim: UPF1 recruitment did not depend on pre-mRNA splicing.
source: UPF1 was recruited both to intron-containing and intronless genes that were undergoing transcription (Figure 5—figure supplement 1, and see also the earlier discussion of heat-shock gene activation), so recruitment did not depend on pre-mRNA splicing.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that UPF1 associates with both intron-containing and intronless genes.

claim: Within intron-containing genes, more UPF1 was associated with exons than with introns.
source: Within intron-containing genes, however, more UPF1 was associated with exons than with introns – as can be seen in the ChIP-seq profiles of highly UPF1-enriched genes such as Xrp1 (Figure 5A; and Figure 5—figure supplement 1 shows other examples of genes displaying this pattern).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ChIP-seq profiles shown in Figure 5A and related figures.

claim: Relatively more of UPF1 is associated with downstream exons than with the first exon at several genes.
source: Additionally, it appears that relatively more of UPF1 is associated with downstream exons than with the first exon, at Xrp1 as well as several of the other genes; notably, in many such cases most of the first exon corresponds to the 5'UTR (see examples in Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ChIP-seq profiles shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The exon-biased UPF1 enrichment was confirmed by real time PCR in multiple ChIP experiments.
source: This exon-biased UPF1 enrichment was confirmed by real time PCR in multiple ChIP experiments (at Xrp1 shown in Figure 5B; and Socs36E, not shown); and it is genome-wide, as demonstrated by comparing UPF1 association with introns and with their flanking exons in the ChIP-seq data from many genes (Figure 5C), UPF1 enrichment is significantly higher for both the left (p=6.737e-8) and the right flanking exon (2.391e-9); for details of how we corrected for possible bias in chromatin fragmentation or sequencing coverage, see Materials and methods.
evidence: This is demonstrated by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The exon-biased UPF1 enrichment is genome-wide.
source: This exon-biased UPF1 enrichment was confirmed by real time PCR in multiple ChIP experiments (at Xrp1 shown in Figure 5B; and Socs36E, not shown); and it is genome-wide, as demonstrated by comparing UPF1 association with introns and with their flanking exons in the ChIP-seq data from many genes (Figure 5C), UPF1 enrichment is significantly higher for both the left (p=6.737e-8) and the right flanking exon (2.391e-9); for details of how we corrected for possible bias in chromatin fragmentation or sequencing coverage, see Materials and methods.
evidence: This is demonstrated by genome-wide analysis of ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: UPF1 enrichment is significantly higher for both the left flanking exon (p=6.737e-8) and the right flanking exon (p=2.391e-9) compared to introns.
source: This exon-biased UPF1 enrichment was confirmed by real time PCR in multiple ChIP experiments (at Xrp1 shown in Figure 5B; and Socs36E, not shown); and it is genome-wide, as demonstrated by comparing UPF1 association with introns and with their flanking exons in the ChIP-seq data from many genes (Figure 5C), UPF1 enrichment is significantly higher for both the left (p=6.737e-8) and the right flanking exon (2.391e-9); for details of how we corrected for possible bias in chromatin fragmentation or sequencing coverage, see Materials and methods.
evidence: This is demonstrated by statistical analysis of ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The normal bias towards UPF1-exon association in Xrp1 was abolished in U1-70K-depleted cells.
source: Consistent with this interpretation, the normal bias towards UPF1-exon association in Xrp1 was abolished in U1-70K-depleted cells but persisted in cells depleted of eIF4AIII or Y14 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C; a similar effect was observed at Socs36E, data not shown); Y14 and eIF4III are two EJC proteins that bind the nascent pre-mRNA but are not likely to play a direct splicing role in Drosophila; see (Choudhury et al., 2016).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ChIP-qPCR data comparing different RNAi conditions shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The bias towards UPF1-exon association persisted in cells depleted of eIF4AIII or Y14.
source: Consistent with this interpretation, the normal bias towards UPF1-exon association in Xrp1 was abolished in U1-70K-depleted cells but persisted in cells depleted of eIF4AIII or Y14 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C; a similar effect was observed at Socs36E, data not shown); Y14 and eIF4III are two EJC proteins that bind the nascent pre-mRNA but are not likely to play a direct splicing role in Drosophila; see (Choudhury et al., 2016).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Y14 and eIF4III are two EJC proteins that bind the nascent pre-mRNA but are not likely to play a direct splicing role in Drosophila.
source: Consistent with this interpretation, the normal bias towards UPF1-exon association in Xrp1 was abolished in U1-70K-depleted cells but persisted in cells depleted of eIF4AIII or Y14 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C; a similar effect was observed at Socs36E, data not shown); Y14 and eIF4III are two EJC proteins that bind the nascent pre-mRNA but are not likely to play a direct splicing role in Drosophila; see (Choudhury et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Genes with the most prominent exon-biased UPF1 enrichment are efficiently co-transcriptionally spliced.
source: Moreover, genes with the most prominent exon-biased UPF1 enrichment, such as Xrp1, are efficiently co-transcriptionally spliced (see the Nascent RNA-seq profile in Figure 5A), whereas genes with no detectable exon-biased UPF1 enrichment, such as CG5059, are poorly co-transcriptionally spliced (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C) and are typically expressed at low levels, as reported (Khodor et al., 2011).
evidence: This is demonstrated by nascent RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Genes with no detectable exon-biased UPF1 enrichment are poorly co-transcriptionally spliced and are typically expressed at low levels.
source: Moreover, genes with the most prominent exon-biased UPF1 enrichment, such as Xrp1, are efficiently co-transcriptionally spliced (see the Nascent RNA-seq profile in Figure 5A), whereas genes with no detectable exon-biased UPF1 enrichment, such as CG5059, are poorly co-transcriptionally spliced (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C) and are typically expressed at low levels, as reported (Khodor et al., 2011).
evidence: This is demonstrated by nascent RNA-seq data and supported by a citation.

claim: Intron recognition interferes with the association of UPF1 with the unspliced nascent transcript.
source: It seems therefore, that intron recognition interferes with the association of UPF1 with the unspliced nascent transcript.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined data showing exon-biased UPF1 enrichment and its dependence on U1 snRNP.

claim: In wild-type cells poly(A) was abundant and fairly evenly distributed throughout the cytoplasm, with relatively little in the nuclei.
source: In wild-type cells poly(A) was abundant and fairly evenly distributed throughout the cytoplasm, as would be expected for mature mRNA, and there was relatively little in the nuclei (Figure 6A, panels I-III).
evidence: This is demonstrated by oligo(dT) FISH data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The nuclei of UPF1-depleted cells retained a substantial amount of poly(A), and the cells appeared to contain less cytoplasmic poly(A) than wild-type cells.
source: By contrast, the nuclei of UPF1-depleted cells retained a substantial amount of poly(A), and the cells appeared to contain less cytoplasmic poly(A) than wild-type cells (Figure 6A, panels IV-VI).
evidence: This is demonstrated by oligo(dT) FISH data comparing wild-type and UPF1-depleted cells.

claim: Much of the nuclear-retained poly(A) in the UPF1-depleted cells formed large cluster(s) in either inter-chromosomal spaces or in surrounding nucleoli.
source: Much of the nuclear-retained poly(A) in the UPF1-depleted cells formed large cluster(s) in either inter-chromosomal spaces (Figure 6A, panel VI, white arrow) or, possibly more frequently, in surrounding nucleoli (yellow arrow) that seemed neither linked to or in the proximity of any specific chromosomal region(s) or defined transcription site(s).
evidence: This is demonstrated by oligo(dT) FISH data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: In salivary glands over-expressing a transgene encoding human UPF1 there was no nuclear poly(A) accumulation.
source: In salivary glands over-expressing a transgene encoding human UPF1 there was no such nuclear poly(A) accumulation (Figure 6A, panels VII-IX); indicating that this phenotype is a direct consequence of the absence of UPF1.
evidence: This is demonstrated by oligo(dT) FISH data in UPF1-RNAi cells expressing human UPF1.

claim: The nuclear poly(A) accumulation phenotype is a direct consequence of the absence of UPF1.
source: In salivary glands over-expressing a transgene encoding human UPF1 there was no such nuclear poly(A) accumulation (Figure 6A, panels VII-IX); indicating that this phenotype is a direct consequence of the absence of UPF1.
evidence: This is inferred from the rescue experiment showing that human UPF1 expression prevents poly(A) accumulation.

claim: No poly(A) accumulation was observed in UPF31 mutant glands, or following RNAi depletion of the EJC components Y14 or MAGO.
source: Additionally, no poly(A) accumulation was observed in UPF31 mutant glands, or following RNAi depletion of the EJC components Y14 or MAGO (unpublished data).
evidence: This is stated as unpublished data from the authors.

claim: Expression of hUPF1 suppressed the apparent smaller size of the salivary glands depleted of the endogenous UPF1.
source: Expression of hUPF1 also suppressed the apparent smaller size of the salivary glands depleted of the endogenous UPF1; these glands were comparable in size to that of wild-type (Figure 6A, panels I and VII vs IV).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing gland sizes in the images shown in Figure 6A.

claim: There was little poly(A) associated with most of the wild-type chromosomes.
source: There was little poly(A) associated with most of the wild-type chromosomes. However, a few interbands – such as 2C at the distal end of the X chromosome (Figure 6B) – showed clear poly(A) signals (Figure 6B, left panel), suggesting that some mature mRNAs that have been cleaved and polyadenylated remain associated, at least briefly, with some transcription sites.
evidence: This is demonstrated by oligo(dT) FISH on polytene chromosomes shown in Figure 6B.

claim: A few interbands such as 2C showed clear poly(A) signals in wild-type chromosomes, suggesting that some mature mRNAs remain associated with some transcription sites.
source: There was little poly(A) associated with most of the wild-type chromosomes. However, a few interbands – such as 2C at the distal end of the X chromosome (Figure 6B) – showed clear poly(A) signals (Figure 6B, left panel), suggesting that some mature mRNAs that have been cleaved and polyadenylated remain associated, at least briefly, with some transcription sites.
evidence: This is demonstrated by oligo(dT) FISH data and the authors' interpretation.

claim: The poly(A) accumulation at 2C in wild-type cells may be a consequence of lack of UPF1 at this transcription site.
source: Additionally, since UPF1 was obviously not associated with 2C (see Figure 3A), the poly(A) accumulation at 2C in wild-type cells may be a consequence of lack of UPF1 at this transcription site.
evidence: This is speculated based on the observation that 2C shows poly(A) accumulation but no UPF1 association.

claim: Both the number of transcriptional sites showing poly(A) accumulation and the amount of poly(A) RNA associated with these sites were strikingly increased in UPF1-depleted cells.
source: Both the number of transcriptional sites showing poly(A) accumulation and the amount of poly(A) RNA associated with these sites were strikingly increased in UPF1-depleted cells (Figure 6B, right panel).
evidence: This is demonstrated by oligo(dT) FISH on polytene chromosomes comparing wild-type and UPF1-depleted cells.

claim: There was no visible poly(A) accumulation at site 5C (Actin5C gene) in wild-type, but this band was obviously fluorescent in UPF1-depleted cells.
source: For example, there was no visible poly(A) accumulation at site 5C, which corresponds to the highly transcribed Actin5C gene, in wild-type, but this band was obviously fluorescent in UPF1-depleted cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated by oligo(dT) FISH on polytene chromosomes shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Site 2B showed a faint poly(A) signal in wild-type glands and a strong signal in UPF1-depleted cells.
source: Another example was site 2B – where constitutively expressed sta and rush are probably the most active genes at this larval stage – which showed a faint poly(A) signal in wild-type glands and a strong signal in UPF1-depleted cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated by oligo(dT) FISH on polytene chromosomes shown in Figure 6B.

claim: UPF1 was clearly associated with transcription sites 2B and 5C on polytene chromosomes and in S2 cells.
source: UPF1 was clearly associated with these transcription sites (2B and 5C) on polytene chromosomes (Figure 3A) and in S2 cells (as detected by ChIP: see Supplementary file 2 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1 for the UPF1 profile of Actin5C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence and ChIP-seq data.

claim: UPF1 plays important role(s) in the release of mRNAs from transcription sites and in their transport out of the nucleus.
source: Cumulatively, the data indicate that UPF1 plays important role(s) in the release of mRNAs from transcription sites and in their transport out of the nucleus (Figure 6C shows a cartoon of a transcription site in either a wild-type or UPF1 depleted cell with or without mRNA retention).
evidence: This is the authors' interpretation of the cumulative data showing poly(A) retention in UPF1-depleted cells.

claim: UPF1 shuttling depends on the ATPase activity of the RNA helicase domain, which is required for the dynamic binding and dissociation of UPF1 from mRNAs in both yeast and mammalian cells.
source: In contrast, we present evidence that UPF1 moves constantly within and between cell compartments, and that this shuttling depends on the ATPase activity of the RNA helicase domain, which is required for the dynamic binding and dissociation of UPF1 from mRNAs in both yeast and mammalian cells (Bhattacharya et al., 2000; Franks et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by the authors' data and citations to studies in yeast and mammalian cells.

claim: UPF1 ATPase domain resides within a region previously thought to contain an atypical nuclear localisation signal in mammalian cells.
source: Notably, UPF1 ATPase domain resides within a region previously thought to contain an atypical nuclear localisation signal in mammalian cells, which when deleted, abolished nuclear UPF1 accumulation following LMB treatment (Mendell et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study in mammalian cells.

claim: Typical UPF1 subcellular distribution is primarily a consequence of its continued association with abundant RNA cargos that are being continuously exported out of the nucleus.
source: However, in view of UPF1 ATPase activity being required for this shuttling, we propose that typical UPF1 subcellular distribution, with more of the protein present in the cytoplasm than in the nucleus, is primarily a consequence of its continued association with abundant RNA cargos that are being continuously exported out of the nucleus.
evidence: This is the authors' proposed interpretation of their data.

claim: The NES-dependent CRM1 export pathway is not a major mRNA nuclear export mechanism in Drosophila nor in other well-studied organisms.
source: The NES-dependent CRM1 export pathway is not a major mRNA nuclear export mechanism in Drosophila nor in other well-studied organisms (Herold et al., 2003; Hutten and Kehlenbach, 2007), yet it is required for the export of vastly more abundant cargos consisting of RNP particles like ribosomal subunits and the signal recognition particle (SRP) (Hutten and Kehlenbach, 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The CRM1 export pathway is required for the export of vastly more abundant cargos consisting of RNP particles like ribosomal subunits and the signal recognition particle (SRP).
source: The NES-dependent CRM1 export pathway is not a major mRNA nuclear export mechanism in Drosophila nor in other well-studied organisms (Herold et al., 2003; Hutten and Kehlenbach, 2007), yet it is required for the export of vastly more abundant cargos consisting of RNP particles like ribosomal subunits and the signal recognition particle (SRP) (Hutten and Kehlenbach, 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: UPF1 might bind with SRP, as it strongly associated with the two loci encoding the 7SL RNA.
source: Our data indicate that UPF1 might bind with SRP, as it strongly associated with the two loci encoding the 7SL RNA (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), which make the SRP scaffold.
evidence: This is inferred from ChIP-seq data showing UPF1 association with 7SL RNA genes.

claim: 7SL RNA makes the SRP scaffold.
source: Our data indicate that UPF1 might bind with SRP, as it strongly associated with the two loci encoding the 7SL RNA (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), which make the SRP scaffold.
evidence: This is established knowledge about SRP structure.

claim: UPF1 may not be binding the individual 40S and 60S subunits, as less UPF1 is detected in the centre of the nucleolus than in the remainder of the nucleus.
source: However, UPF1 may not be binding the individual 40S and 60S subunits, as less UPF1 is detected in the centre of the nucleolus than in the remainder of the nucleus - discussed further below.
evidence: This is inferred from the immunofluorescence data showing UPF1 exclusion from the nucleolus center.

claim: Splicing might enhance UPF1 binding, particularly with downstream exons.
source: Splicing might enhance UPF1 binding, particularly with downstream exons (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B, Model 1), however, since UPF1 also associates with intron-less genes, splicing may not be necessary for its loading on nascent transcripts.
evidence: This is one of two models proposed by the authors to explain the data.

claim: Since UPF1 also associates with intron-less genes, splicing may not be necessary for its loading on nascent transcripts.
source: Splicing might enhance UPF1 binding, particularly with downstream exons (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B, Model 1), however, since UPF1 also associates with intron-less genes, splicing may not be necessary for its loading on nascent transcripts.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that UPF1 associates with intronless genes.

claim: UPF1 associates with all Pol II nascent transcripts, but on intron-containing pre-mRNAs, splice site recognition interferes with intron binding.
source: Possibly, UPF1 associates with all Pol II nascent transcripts, but on intron-containing pre-mRNAs, splice site recognition interferes with intron binding.
evidence: This is the authors' proposed interpretation of their data.

claim: UPF1 scanning of pre-mRNAs may influence 5' splice sites recognition and affect splicing directly.
source: UPF1 scanning of pre-mRNAs may therefore influence 5' splice sites recognition and affect splicing directly; changes in the relative concentrations of many alternatively spliced transcripts have been reported in UPF1-depleted S2 cells (Brooks et al., 2015).
evidence: This is speculated based on the authors' data and supported by a citation to a study showing splicing changes in UPF1-depleted cells.

claim: Changes in the relative concentrations of many alternatively spliced transcripts have been reported in UPF1-depleted S2 cells.
source: UPF1 scanning of pre-mRNAs may therefore influence 5' splice sites recognition and affect splicing directly; changes in the relative concentrations of many alternatively spliced transcripts have been reported in UPF1-depleted S2 cells (Brooks et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Simple affinity of UPF1 for RNA is not likely to be the primary reason why UPF1 associates with some nascent transcripts.
source: Simple affinity of UPF1 for RNA is not likely to be the primary reason why UPF1 associates with some nascent transcripts, for several reasons: UPF1 does not associate with some highly transcribed Pol II genes, such as spliceosomal snRNAs; nor with snRNA U6 or other highly active Pol III genes; nor with rRNA genes transcribed by Pol I; there would be no differential affinity for introns vs. exons within a transcript; and UPF1 appears to be excluded from the RNA-packed centre of the nucleolus where rRNA genes are transcribed and ribosomal subunits are assembled (McLeod et al., 2014).
evidence: This is the authors' interpretation based on multiple observations from their data.

claim: One possible candidate feature that dictates UPF1 association would be the 7-methylguanosine (m7G) cap that is added co-transcriptionally to the 5'end of pre-mRNAs but not to Pol I and Pol III transcripts.
source: What features of some nascent transcripts, most often of Pol II-transcribed genes, dictate that UPF1 becomes associated with them remain to be determined. One possible candidate would be the 7-methylguanosine (m7G) cap that is added co-transcriptionally to the 5'end of pre-mRNAs but not to Pol I and Pol III transcripts (Ghosh and Lima, 2010).
evidence: This is speculation by the authors, supported by a citation about cap structure.

claim: The m7G caps added to snRNAs and other small non-mRNA Pol II transcripts are further modified by hypermethylation to generate 2,2,7-trimethylguanosine(m(3)G) structures.
source: Moreover, the m7G caps added to snRNAs and other small non-mRNA Pol II transcripts are further modified though by hypermethylation to generate 2,2,7-trimethylguanosine(m(3)G) structures (Mouaikel et al., 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Hypermethylation of snRNA caps occurs after the transcripts have been exported to the cytoplasm in mammalian cells.
source: Although this hypermethylation occurs after the transcripts have been exported to the cytoplasm in mammalian cells, perhaps this modification may occur in the nucleus instead in other organisms (Mouaikel et al., 2002), and this might explain why these classes of transcripts are not associated with UPF1 in Drosophila.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Hypermethylation of snRNA caps might occur in the nucleus in organisms other than mammals, which might explain why these classes of transcripts are not associated with UPF1 in Drosophila.
source: Although this hypermethylation occurs after the transcripts have been exported to the cytoplasm in mammalian cells, perhaps this modification may occur in the nucleus instead in other organisms (Mouaikel et al., 2002), and this might explain why these classes of transcripts are not associated with UPF1 in Drosophila.
evidence: This is speculation by the authors to explain their observations.

claim: The association of UPF1 with nascent transcripts seems to be dynamic.
source: The association of UPF1 with nascent transcripts seems to be dynamic, and its putative 5'-to-3' scanning along RNA is likely to be fast and, at least on intron-containing pre-mRNAs, discontinuous.
evidence: This is inferred from the FRAP/FLIP data and the exon-biased enrichment pattern.

claim: UPF1's putative 5'-to-3' scanning along RNA is likely to be fast and, at least on intron-containing pre-mRNAs, discontinuous.
source: The association of UPF1 with nascent transcripts seems to be dynamic, and its putative 5'-to-3' scanning along RNA is likely to be fast and, at least on intron-containing pre-mRNAs, discontinuous.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing exon-biased enrichment and rapid mobility.

claim: When UPF1 encounters a steric block that cannot be removed, it must be capable of quickly dissociating and re-loading elsewhere on the transcript.
source: This pattern also suggests that when it encounters a steric block that cannot be removed, UPF1 must be capable of quickly dissociating and re-loading elsewhere on the transcript.
evidence: This is inferred from the discontinuous enrichment pattern observed in the data.

claim: In vitro, UPF1 can translocate along RNAs over long distances but only at a maximum scanning velocity of ~80 base/min.
source: In vitro, UPF1 can translocate along RNAs over long distances – but only at a maximum scanning velocity of ~80 base/min (Fiorini et al., 2015), which is much slower than the 2–3 kb/min of Pol II (Fiorini et al., 2015; Fukaya et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge from in vitro studies, supported by citations.

claim: The maximum scanning velocity of UPF1 (~80 base/min) is much slower than the 2–3 kb/min of Pol II.
source: In vitro, UPF1 can translocate along RNAs over long distances – but only at a maximum scanning velocity of ~80 base/min (Fiorini et al., 2015), which is much slower than the 2–3 kb/min of Pol II (Fiorini et al., 2015; Fukaya et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: UPF1 either translocates along RNA faster in vivo, or its scanning is not processive as envisaged, or it is piggybacking on another entity that is capable of translocating on the RNA faster than UPF1.
source: Therefore, UPF1 either translocates along RNA faster in vivo, or its scanning is not processive as envisaged, or it is factually piggybacking on another entity that is capable of translocating on the RNA faster than UPF1.
evidence: This is speculation by the authors to reconcile the slow in vitro rate with the observed in vivo association.

claim: The machinery that UPF1 might piggyback on is unlikely to be the Pol II itself, as there is no evidence of a strong direct association of Pol II with UPF1.
source: Although this machinery is unlikely to be the Pol II itself, as we found no evidence of a strong direct association of Pol II with UPF1.
evidence: This is inferred from the authors' data showing weak co-IP of UPF1 with Pol II.

claim: Less of UPF1 is associated with the 5' proximal region of nascent transcripts, which, in some instances, coincides with the 5'UTR.
source: Notably, we observed that less of UPF1 is associated with the 5' proximal region of nascent transcripts, which, in some instances, coincides with the 5'UTR (see Actin5C in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ChIP-seq profiles shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: 5'UTRs are defined by the process of translation initiation, in which the 40S migrates downstream until it recognises the start codon.
source: 5'UTRs are defined by the process of translation initiation, in which, following association with the mRNA's 5' cap, the 40S (carrying the initiator tRNA) migrates downstream until it recognises the start codon (Kozak, 1989).
evidence: This is established knowledge about translation initiation, supported by a citation.

claim: Less association of UPF1 with 5'UTRs might signify that its binding to nascent transcripts is translation dependent, at least in some instances.
source: Less association of UPF1 with 5'UTRs might therefore signify that its binding to nascent transcripts is translation dependent, at least in some instances, and supports the view that ribosomes start scanning mRNAs cotranscriptionally; evidence of which has previously been reported in Drosophila (Al-Jubran et al., 2013; Brogna et al., 2002).
evidence: This is speculation by the authors based on their observation, supported by citations to studies showing cotranscriptional translation.

claim: Evidence of ribosomes starting to scan mRNAs cotranscriptionally has previously been reported in Drosophila.
source: Less association of UPF1 with 5'UTRs might therefore signify that its binding to nascent transcripts is translation dependent, at least in some instances, and supports the view that ribosomes start scanning mRNAs cotranscriptionally; evidence of which has previously been reported in Drosophila (Al-Jubran et al., 2013; Brogna et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies in Drosophila.

claim: Mature mRNAs that have been cleaved and polyadenylated are normally expected to be speedily released from transcription sites.
source: Mature mRNAs that have been cleaved and polyadenylated are normally expected to be speedily released from transcription sites, but our data show that this is not always the case.
evidence: This is the prevailing expectation in the field, which the authors' data challenge.

claim: Some sites on polytene chromosomes apparently accumulate poly(A) RNA even in wild-type glands.
source: We have both: a) identified some sites on polytene chromosomes that apparently accumulate poly(A) RNA even in wild-type glands; and b) shown that most of the active Pol II genes accumulate poly(A) RNA in UPF1-depleted salivary glands.
evidence: This is demonstrated by oligo(dT) FISH data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Most of the active Pol II genes accumulate poly(A) RNA in UPF1-depleted salivary glands.
source: We have both: a) identified some sites on polytene chromosomes that apparently accumulate poly(A) RNA even in wild-type glands; and b) shown that most of the active Pol II genes accumulate poly(A) RNA in UPF1-depleted salivary glands.
evidence: This is demonstrated by oligo(dT) FISH data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Poly(A) RNA accumulation in UPF1-depleted cells is most prominent at genes with which UPF1 associates strongly in wild-type.
source: Poly(A) RNA accumulation in UPF1-depleted cells is most prominent at genes with which UPF1 associates strongly in wild-type, such as Actin5C (shown both microscopically and by ChIP-seq).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing ChIP-seq data and oligo(dT) FISH data.

claim: Evidence of retention of poly(A) and specific mRNAs in discrete nuclear foci or 'dots' has previously been reported in cells defective in RNA processing.
source: Evidence of retention of poly(A) and specific mRNAs in discrete nuclear foci or 'dots' has previously been reported in cells defective in RNA processing, initially in mRNA export and processing mutants in yeast (Jensen et al., 2001); and later in other cells in which one of several RNA processing reactions are impaired (Abruzzi et al., 2006; Paul and Montpetit, 2016), including Drosophila cells carrying mutation in the RNA helicase P68 (Buszczak and Spradling, 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: UPF1 plays an important genome-wide role in the release of mRNAs from transcription sites and their export to the cytoplasm, at least in Drosophila salivary gland cells.
source: In summary, our results indicate that UPF1 plays an important genome-wide role in the release of mRNAs from transcription sites and their export to the cytoplasm, at least in Drosophila salivary gland cells.
evidence: This is the authors' conclusion based on their cumulative data.

claim: In the absence of UPF1 function, mRNPs may acquire or retain native conformations that hinder their release from the chromosome and make them prone to aggregation and nuclear retention.
source: Possibly, in the absence of UPF1 function, mRNPs acquire or retain native conformations that hinder their release from the chromosome and make them prone to aggregation and, consequently, cause nuclear retention.
evidence: This is speculation by the authors to explain the mechanism behind their observations.

claim: A global role of UPF1 in mRNA release and export could explain why this protein is universally conserved in eukaryotes.
source: Such a global role of UPF1 could explain, better than its involvement in NMD, why this protein is universally conserved in eukaryotes, why its depletion affects the expression of a large fraction of the genome, and possibly why expression of human UPF1 in rat models of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) overcomes the pathology caused by over-expression or mutation of the RNA-binding protein TDP-43 (Barmada et al., 2015; Jackson et al., 2015).
evidence: This is the authors' interpretation of the broader implications of their findings.

claim: Expression of human UPF1 in rat models of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) overcomes the pathology caused by over-expression or mutation of the RNA-binding protein TDP-43.
source: Such a global role of UPF1 could explain, better than its involvement in NMD, why this protein is universally conserved in eukaryotes, why its depletion affects the expression of a large fraction of the genome, and possibly why expression of human UPF1 in rat models of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) overcomes the pathology caused by over-expression or mutation of the RNA-binding protein TDP-43 (Barmada et al., 2015; Jackson et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies in ALS models.
